extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and graduate students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a combinatorics textbook chapter presenting definitions and theorems in enumerative combinatorics: V-partitions and related generating functions, the sieve (inclusion–exclusion) approach, the involution principle (and its variants), and the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot determinantal method for nonintersecting lattice paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: V-partitions and v(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: A V-partition is a unimodal sequence “rooted” at one of its largest parts. Let v(n) be the number of V-partitions of n, with v(0)=1. Example: v(4)=12 (list of rooted unimodal sequences of 4 is given). The generating function V(q)=∑_{n≥0} v(n) q^n = 1 + q + 3q^2 + 6q^3 + 12q^4 + ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: V-partitions are described concretely by arrays of parts (with the root specified). The chapter presents both counting examples and the generating-series viewpoint (V(q)). A product or other closed form for V(q) is sought and motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Double partitions and d(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dn denotes the set of all double partitions of n (arrays with two rows a_i, b_i satisfying specified weakly decreasing inequalities); d(n) = #Dn and d(n) has an associated generating function (equation (2.28) in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double partitions are introduced as an auxiliary combinatorial class used to count V-partitions via maps Γ1, Γ2, ... from Dn to subsets of Vn. The relations between Dn and Vn (surjective maps that are not injective) are used to derive sieve relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieve-theoretic relation between v(n) and d(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: v(n) = d(n) − d(n−1) + d(n−3) − d(n−6) + ⋯, with the convention d(m)=0 for m<0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alternating sum arises from iteratively defining surjective maps Γ1, Γ2, ... from Dn to progressively restricted subsets of Vn; each Γi double-counts certain V-partitions so the sieve (inclusion–exclusion) alternating sum corrects for overcounting. This relation is used to derive Proposition 2.5.1 giving a generating-function expression for V(q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function identity relating unimodal sequences: U(q)+V(q)=∏_{i≥1}(1−q^i)^{-2}
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 2.5.2 states that the generating functions U(q) (for unimodal sequences) and V(q) (for rooted unimodal sequences) satisfy U(q) + V(q) = ∏_{i≥1} (1−q^i)^{-2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bijection between Dn and Un ∪ Vn is provided in the proof; the identity follows by equating generating functions. This identity and its corollary give explicit product/sieve-type formulae for U(q) and V(q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: explicit expression for U(q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 2.5.3 gives an explicit series/product expression for U(q) derived from the previous propositions (an explicit form is stated in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U(q) is obtained from U(q)+V(q) and the formula for V(q); the corollary records the closed-form generating function used elsewhere in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution principle (basic form) — hypotheses (a) and (b) and weight identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose finite set X is partitioned X = X^+ ∪ X^−. Let τ be an involution on X satisfying: (a) if τ(x)=y and x≠y then exactly one of x,y is in X^+ (the other is in X^−); (b) if τ(x)=x then x∈X^+. Define weight w(x)=1 for x∈X^+, w(x)=−1 for x∈X^−. Then #Fix(τ) = ∑_{x∈X} w(x) (equation (2.31)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The involution cancels pairs of elements of opposite sign, leaving fixed points which are all positive; the weight sum therefore equals the number of fixed points. This encapsulates a standard combinatorial proof technique that turns alternating sums into counts of fixed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution principle — canonical bijection between fixed-point sets under sign-preserving bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: Given another set X˜ with corresponding partition and involution τ˜, and a sign-preserving bijection f: X→X˜, there is a canonical bijection g between Fix(τ) and Fix(τ˜) defined by g(x)=f (τ f^{-1} τ˜ f)^n(x), where n is the least nonnegative integer for which the expression stabilizes (equation (2.32)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction is illustrated graphically (components of a graph Γ) and guarantees Fix(τ) and Fix(τ˜) have same size; it is a general mechanism to convert involution-based equalities into explicit bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieve-equivalence variation and bijection h between set-differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given finite sets X and Y with Y⊆X and bijections f:X→X and g:Y→Y satisfying certain disjointness conditions (#(X−Y)=#(X−Y˜) etc.), one may construct an explicit bijection h between X−Y and X−Y˜ via repeated compositions f(g^{-1} f)^n(x) where n is the least integer making the element lie outside Y (equation (2.33)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variation is used to build explicit bijections in cases of equal cardinalities resulting from PIE-type arguments. Example 2.6.1 shows the construction for permutations with exactly one cycle and those fixing 1, producing a concrete h.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: lattice-path weight and complete-homogeneous-function h(m;γ,δ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For lattice paths in N^2, assign weight x_j to a horizontal step from (i,j)→(i+1,j); the weight Λ(L) of a path is the product of weights of its horizontal steps. For a path from (β_i,γ_i) to (α_i,δ_i) with m=α_i−β_i horizontal steps, h(m;γ_i,δ_i)=sum_{k1≥...≥km, δ_i≤kj≤γ_i} x_{k1}...x_{km}, i.e., the complete homogeneous symmetric function h_m taken on variables x_{δ_i},...,x_{γ_i} (equation (2.36)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This weight convention and the function h(m;γ,δ) let one express generating sums for families of paths in algebraic form suited to determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot determinantal theorem for nonintersecting n-paths (Theorem 2.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A(α,β,γ,δ) be the sum of weights of all n-paths of type (α,β,γ,δ) and let B(α,β,γ,δ) be the sum over nonintersecting n-paths. Under mild monotonicity hypotheses on α,β,γ,δ (β_i<β_{i+1}, γ_i≤γ_{i+1}, δ_i≤δ_{i+1}) and the condition that A(w(α),β,γ,w(δ)) is empty unless w is the identity, the theorem states B(α,β,γ,δ) = det[ h(α_j − β_i; γ_i, δ_j) ]_{1≤i,j≤n} (equation (2.37)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof expands the determinant as ∑_{w∈S_n} sgn(w) A(w(α),β,γ,w(δ)) and then constructs a sign-reversing, weight-preserving involution ∗ on intersecting n-paths pairing them so only contributions of nonintersecting paths remain. This is a fundamental tool linking determinants and nonintersecting path enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the involution * on intersecting n-paths (weight-preserving, sign-reversing pairing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an intersecting n-path L, pick the least i for which Li intersects some L_k (k≠i), then the least x-coordinate x of an intersection with k>i, and among such k pick the minimum j; form L* by swapping tails of Li and Lj at their first intersection point v=(x,y); for other indices paths are unchanged. Then (a) ∗ is an involution, (b) Λ(L*)=Λ(L) (weight-preserving), (c) the permutation indexing the terminal points is multiplied by transposition (i,j) so signs are opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canonical choice of (i,j,v) ensures pairwise cancellation of contributions of intersecting path configurations in the determinant expansion; only nonintersecting configurations survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: counting nonintersecting lattice paths via determinant (Example 2.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For paths between specified start/end points avoiding a set S, choose α,β,γ,δ as indicated in the example and set all x_m=1. Then f(r,s,S) (number of nonintersecting paths) equals B(α,β,γ,δ), which by Theorem 2.7.1 equals a determinant whose entries (with x_m=1) evaluate to simple binomial-type numbers; the determinant expansion gives a PIE-style formula for f(r,s,S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates how the determinant formulation specializes to classical counting formulas (and can be rearranged to a PIE expression or specialized to known determinant evaluations).

rubrics_metrics.name: General methodological principle: use bijections and involutions to convert algebraic identities into combinatorial proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the chapter the recommended method to prove equalities of alternating sums or generating-function identities is to produce explicit bijections or involutions that pair terms to cancel and identify fixed points; the involution principle and sieve-equivalence are formalizations of this approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text supplies canonical constructions (σ in Section 2.6, the ∗ involution in Section 2.7, Γ_i maps earlier) and visualizations (graphs of components) to turn non-combinatorial algebraic identities into bijective/combinatorial proofs. Exercises ask reader to carry out these constructions in specific enumerative problems.
